name: Germinal centre B cell
markers: AID (inside the cell; the enzyme that mutates antibody genes)
CXCR4 high in the dark zone; CD83 and CD86 high in the light zone
summary: A B cell that has been activated by antigen and helper T cells and now divides inside a germinal centre. It mutates its antibody genes at random (somatic hypermutation), then tests the new antibody against antigen. Cells whose antibody binds better survive and keep dividing or leave as plasma cells or memory B cells. The rest die.
functions: Starts the germinal centre: a few activated B cells (shown in mice to be a small number of founder clones) move into the middle of a follicle and divide rapidly.

In the dark zone divides every few hours, and the enzyme AID introduces point mutations into its antibody genes at a rate far above the rest of the genome (somatic hypermutation), producing many slightly different antibodies.

In the light zone tests its new antibody against antigen held on follicular dendritic cells. Cells that bind badly receive no help and die by apoptosis; cells that bind well take up antigen and show it on MHC class II to Tfh cells.

Cycles between the two zones many times. The amount of Tfh help it wins sets how many more rounds of division it undergoes, so antibody affinity rises over weeks (affinity maturation). This was worked out mainly in mice.
Switches antibody class (class-switch recombination), also through AID, from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE. Cytokines from Tfh cells and others help choose the class.
Leaves as a plasma cell or a memory B cell. In mice, cells that leave early tend to become memory cells and those that leave late plasma cells.
Debated: what decides between plasma cell and memory B cell. Higher-affinity cells appear biased toward plasma cells, but lower-affinity cells also become memory cells.
Debated: how strongly a germinal centre selects the single best clone. In mice, many germinal centres stay diverse and keep lower-affinity clones alongside the best.
In humans, germinal centres have been sampled from lymph nodes by fine-needle aspiration after vaccination, where they persisted for months. Most of the detailed dynamics come from mice.
abundance: Absent from blood and from resting lymph nodes. A germinal centre forms about a week after immunisation or infection and lasts weeks to months. In human tonsils, which are constantly responding to microbes, germinal centre B cells are a substantial minority of the B cells.
